analysis.one_liner: Creates a three-year federal backstop requiring insurers to keep selling terrorism coverage after attacks.
analysis.headline: The bill became law on November 26, 2002 as Public Law 107-297, after passing the House 227-193 and the Senate 86-11, giving insurers a federal backstop covering 90% of terrorism losses up to $100 billion a year.
analysis.plain_summary: After the September 11 attacks, insurers began writing terrorism out of commercial policies, which threatened to freeze construction, real estate deals, and lending. This bill created a three-year federal backstop: insurers had to keep offering terrorism coverage, and if an attack happened, the Treasury would pay 90% of insured losses above the insurers' own deductibles, up to $100 billion a year, with part of that repaid through surcharges on commercial insurance premiums. It also let victims of terrorism seize frozen assets of terrorists and state sponsors to pay court judgments, and made small changes to Federal Reserve emergency-lending rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses large and small that buy commercial property insurance, construction projects, landlords, and lenders, who would otherwise have faced dropped coverage or steep premium spikes for terrorism risk after 9/11. Workers are covered too, because workers' compensation policies are included, meaning terrorism coverage stays available for injuries on the job. Victims of state-sponsored terrorism gain a way to seize frozen foreign assets to satisfy court judgments.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Businesses, landlords, construction projects, and workers

how_it_helps.text: Requires every commercial property and casualty insurer to make terrorism coverage available in all policies, including workers' compensation, on terms not materially different from coverage for other perils.

Has the Treasury pay 90% of insured terrorism losses above each insurer's deductible, which starts at 1% of the insurer's premiums and rises to 15% by the third year, capped at $100 billion in federal payments per year.

Voids terrorism exclusions already written into existing policies unless the policyholder affirmatively agrees in writing to reinstate the exclusion, and requires insurers to disclose the terrorism premium as a separate line item.

Allows victims of terrorism to attach frozen assets of terrorists, terrorist organizations, and state sponsors of terrorism to satisfy compensatory damage judgments, with a special payment schedule for judgment holders with claims against Iran.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers stand behind up to $100 billion a year in federal payments, counted as emergency spending outside normal budget limits. Commercial insurance policyholders bear the first losses through premiums and, if an attack's losses stay below the program's retention thresholds, a surcharge of up to 3% of their premiums to repay the federal government. State regulators lose some authority: state rate-approval requirements are suspended for terrorism rates and state laws that block insurers from recovering federal assessments through premiums are preempted.

drawbacks.text: Commits taxpayers to pay 90% of qualifying losses above insurer deductibles, up to $100 billion a year, designated as emergency spending under budget law.

When losses stay below the industry retention amounts ($10 billion to $15 billion depending on the year), the mandatory repayment of federal assistance comes from a surcharge of up to 3% of premiums charged to commercial policyholders, not from insurer profits.

Repayment beyond that mandatory amount is discretionary, with the Treasury told to weigh insurers' profitability and the affordability of insurance for small businesses, so a large share of any federal payout may never be recovered from the industry.
The Treasury Secretary's certification of an act of terrorism and other payment determinations are final and cannot be reviewed by any court.

Preempts state insurance regulation in several ways, including suspending state prior-approval of terrorism rates and nullifying state-approved terrorism exclusions, shifting decisions from state regulators to the federal Treasury.
Includes a provision letting the Federal Reserve Board act on emergency lending with fewer members than normally required if the rest cannot be reached.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For its moment — the months after 9/11, when insurers were stripping terrorism coverage from commercial policies and threatening to halt construction and lending — the bill did real public good: coverage stayed available, projects went forward, and workers kept terrorism protection in their compensation policies. But the structure leans toward insurers. They keep the premiums collected for terrorism coverage while the federal government takes 90% of the catastrophic losses above their deductibles, and the repayment designed into the bill falls mostly on policyholder surcharges rather than insurer profits. A well-designed backstop would have put more of the industry's own capital at risk before taxpayer money; the rising deductibles partially address this, but the industry came out well ahead of the public purse in the bargain.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed its version 227-193 a few weeks after 9/11; the Senate threw out that text, substituted its own bill, and passed it by unanimous consent in July 2002; a conference committee merged the two, both chambers approved the result (the Senate 86-11 after an 85-12 vote to end debate), and President Bush signed it on November 26, 2002.

narrative.text: Introduced on November 1, 2001 by House Financial Services Chairman Michael Oxley, three weeks after the September 11 attacks, to address insurers' withdrawal of terrorism coverage.

The House Financial Services and Ways and Means Committees reported the bill within three weeks, and the House passed it 227-193 on November 29, 2001, with 207 of 220 voting Republicans in favor and only 19 of 211 voting Democrats.

Before passage, House Democrats' attempt to amend the bill failed 173-243; the amendment would have struck the litigation-management section and stopped insurers from passing program costs through to customers.
The Senate laid the House bill aside, replaced its text with its own version (S. 2600), and passed that by unanimous consent on July 25, 2002.

The House voted 373-0 on September 10, 2002 to instruct its conferees to accept the Senate's provision letting victims satisfy judgments from frozen assets of terrorists and state sponsors of terrorism.

The conference report passed the House by voice vote on November 14, 2002 and the Senate on November 20, 2002 by 86-11, after cloture on debate was invoked 85-12, with all 49 Democrats, both independents, and 34 of 49 Republicans in favor.
President Bush signed the bill into law on November 26, 2002 as Public Law 107-297.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Commercial insurers gained most: they kept collecting terrorism premiums while the federal government took on 90% of catastrophic losses above their deductibles, and the Democratic attempts to strike the litigation-management section and bar insurers from passing costs to customers failed. Commercial landlords, developers, and lenders also came out ahead because terrorism coverage stayed available through the post-9/11 market disruption.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Commercial insurers and large property owners

sides.party_line_note: House passage in November 2001 split sharply by party — 207 of 220 voting Republicans yes versus 19 of 211 voting Democrats yes — but the Senate later passed its version by unanimous consent and approved the conference report with all 49 Democrats and 35 of 49 Republicans in favor.

industries.note: The bill forces insurers to sell terrorism coverage, but it also makes them the permanent channel for that risk with a federal backstop paying 90% of losses above their deductibles, while insurers keep the premiums and most repayment can come from policyholder surcharges rather than insurer profits. Taxpayers absorb the catastrophic tail that the industry could not or would not price.

The federal backstop reduced insurers' need to buy terrorism reinsurance, but the bill expressly allows insurers to reinsure their own deductibles and retained losses without reducing their federal compensation, and Congress commissioned studies on whether a private reinsurance pool could eventually replace the program.

industries.industry: Commercial real estate, construction, and lenders
industries.note: With insurers excluding terrorism after 9/11, projects, leases, and construction lending were at risk; guaranteed availability of coverage prevented premium spikes and coverage gaps. The bill also preempts state laws that would have blocked insurers from recovering federal assessments through premiums, so some cost flows back to commercial tenants and buyers.

industries.industry: Municipalities and self-insured entities, including state workers' compensation funds
industries.note: State residual market entities and workers' compensation funds are brought under the program by regulation, gaining a federal backstop but also owing deductibles and possible surcharges; municipalities can opt in only by a determination made before an attack occurs.
